On that day, Jimmy, in Newark, when people started calling, like Quincy Jones or whoever – I think a lot of people called – and it all began because it was reported on the radio that you were dead. Here you are talking on the radio. You come down to the station. You get some gigs. Did it renew your spirit?
Yes, it helped a lot. It helped a lot.

It helped to renew your spirit. Then another part of your career begins, where you’re playing little clubs, like the Baby Grand, like you were saying, in Long Island and all over, but you’re still struggling, but you’re able to make a humble living as a jazz singer. Is that accurate?
No. It wasn’t enough. I wasn’t able to make a steady living . . .
Ah. That’s the distinction that has to be made.
. . . a steady income . . .
There was no steady income.

. . . that would support me until things got in shape or I could find someone who could handle things for me. I had a sister who lived there, but they never – none of my folks ever wanted to be around me. I have never had any of them at a performance of mine. No-one in the family. What are you going to do? So I couldn’t talk to them about the business end, because they had to come around.
Do you know – tell me about – because this is an important character in the new phase of your career – tell me when you first met Doc Pomus, the great . . .
At the Baby Grand. The funniest thing, he had a metal brace . . .
On his leg.
. . . on his leg.
This is Doc Pomus, the great blues composer and singer.
Right, and writer. Anyway, Doc used to come to the Baby Grand.
This is in the late 1940s.

Anyhow, he was sitting in the chair, and this brace was reflecting light. He would move his foot or something, and the lights would reflect. I kept seeing this. Then I realized, that’s that thing on his leg. That’s how we met, because when I’d come off, I knew who he was. I go over and greet him. We sat and talked and became friends. I even was invited to his house. Ertugun – Nes Ertugun – it wasn’t Ertugun – his brother? What is it?
Raoul.
Raoul, yeah.
Felder.
Oh boy. He didn’t like it, because . . .
The lawyer.
. . . yeah. He didn’t like it, because Doc Pomus brought me to his house, and I had dinner with him. He didn’t like it. Very nasty.

The record industry, for not giving Jimmy Scott a record deal. He says, “What’s wrong with you guys? This is one of the greatest vocalists there is out there. Why don’t you give him a deal? This is crazy. He is going to die, and everybody’s going to say how great he was, and he’ll never have a deal.” Tell me your reaction. Did you read that letter in Billboard? Or did you learn about it?
No, I didn’t.
So you didn’t even know that it happened.
No, I didn’t.
Because you weren’t even reading Billboard then. Neither was I.
He would call my house. Keep up with me. “How you doing, Jim?” I said, “Good.” Until the end. That last call I got, the person that called told me he passed.
Now we’re in the early ’90s. When you were invited to perform at Doc’s funeral, you had no hesitancy.
No.
You were going to do it.
I did it.
Tell me about that funeral.
It was highly sad in many ways, and a lot of people felt that sadness.
Do you remember what song you sang?
Uh . . .
Somebody to Watch over Me, wasn’t it?
Someone to Watch over Me. You’re right.
Tell us what happened after the funeral.
Huh?
Tell us what happened after the funeral.
Everybody went their own way. I got on the train and went back to Newark, because I was living in Newark at the time. I had an apartment there. I went on back to Newark.
When was the first time that you heard, as a result of your performance at the funeral, there was interest in you as a recording artist again?
Interest?

I’ll ask it again. When was the first time, after the funeral, you heard that there was interest in you as a recording artist – that people were beginning to talk about recording you, because they had heard you do Somebody to Watch over Me at the funeral? When did that happen? Who called you?
It was a little reporter that lived in Brooklyn. He called and told me what was going on.
Then did you hear from Seymour Stein? Did he call you? Or you don’t recall that?
I don’t recall.
Because what I’m trying to figure out is how – what led to making the album All the Way with Tommy LiPuma?

Actually, the attention came from the funeral. The attention came from the funeral, and they got together and got him. I think he did a good job for the recording, helping to produce the recording. I think Tommy did a good job.

Did you think – was all this taking you by surprise? Because it had been so long since you had had a record deal. To get a recording contract from Warner Bros. Records, which is a huge label, as a result of singing at the funeral and having Seymour Stein – who was a big-shot music mogul – hear you and able to give you a contract, and then give you one of the leading jazz producers in the country, must have been a big thrill? Or were you excited?
It was for me, yeah.
You were excited by that.
You get excited . . .
But you’re scared it . . .
. . . and you always hope that this is it.
Right. That’s what I’m saying. But you had been excited before and been disappointed, so you . . .
Yes.
. . . you keep your expectations down.
There you go. You’re fighting to keep from getting excited over things.
Knowing that your heart might be broken, and you don’t want to deal with another broken heart.
Yeah, right. So many times.
So many times. So many times.
You’ve got the idea. You’re right dead-on the idea.
You want to keep your expectations down, because you don’t want your heart broken again.
Right.
Tell about – again, the – when, in picking out the tunes and all, was that a happy experience? Were you involved artistically in the making of that album?
Yes.
So nobody imposed material on you that you don’t want to do.
No. We created the songs, myself and Tommy, with his suggestions and his ideas. He put it over beautifully. I got to give it to him.
As a result, in the ’90s you were able to find some work and be rediscovered by a group of people, one of whom was Lou Reed. How did you meet Lou Reed?
They were coming to the club.
I think Doc was friends with Lou.

Yeah. They’d come over to see Doc and hang with him. That was because Doc was a writer. Lou liked his work and would try get Doc to write songs for him. I think Doc gave it up and never did another tune for him.
When Lou asked you to tour with him – was that a surprise for you, when Lou Reed . . .?
Yeah. I’m – what is this?
What is this?! Did you even know what his music was like?

See, Lou is gay, and he wanted to mess around. That wasn’t my thing. I wasn’t into that crap. Okay? I knew many that were, but no, not me. No. So I had to tell him, take it another way, because it ain’t here. This ain’t the stuff.
What was the music like on that tour, going to England and Europe? How was your music received? Or did you sing his music?
Beautiful. I think he got jealous, because of the response that I got from the audience. He began acting funny.
Haughty?

So I said, oh, well, okay, because I’ve seen it before. It wasn’t like I hadn’t seen that before. So I went on about my business, and Lou went on about his. But Lou still tries to come around and make me think like he thinks. It’ll never happen. It hasn’t happened all these years. So it’ll never happen, baby. No, baby, they can take that gay mess and keep it to themselves. God bless ’em.
So you come back after being on the road with Lou. Then, this is also this period of time when you get a lot of national exposure, isn’t it? – when you appear in the David Byrne television show.
Yes.
What’s that called again?
Jeannie Scott: [inaudible]
Sessions at 54 – no, but I was thinking about the t.v. show, that big-time t.v. show. Jimmy Scott: Oh yeah. He had a different name for the t.v. show.
Yeah. You know, the famous show. It was a cult t.v. show. He was on the final episode. Jeannie Scott: “Twin Peaks.”
Yeah, “Twin Peaks,” because that always killed me. Jeannie Scott: That’s David Lynch.
I mean David Lynch. Forgive me. David Byrne . . . Jimmy Scott: What was the name of it?
David Lynch, the director. It’s my mind turning to mush. David Lynch, who had you on the episode, the concluding episode of “Twin Peaks.” What was that like? How did that come about?

I was accepted quite well and supported beautifully with the band. Then they had me come in and do something with strings – with the band, but strings were added. I don’t know what they ever did with those records.
Oh yeah. It would be good to have them, because they never came out.
No.
Then you have this long – or at least three- or four-, five-years period where you get a recording contract with Fantasy and you do these albums produced by . . .
Yeah. That was . . .
Todd Barkin.
. . . Todd Barkin. Yeah.
Tell us about those albums and . . .
Todd was skunky too. He was one of them skunks that they didn’t want to do right and you were supposed to accept it, because they were who they were.
Because – but your feeling about that was that they didn’t give you the artistic freedom, they didn’t let you pick the . . .
They didn’t respect you.
I see.
They didn’t respect your ability. Everything turned out to be nothing.

On the personal tip here – one thing I’d like to get in here, because we haven’t talked about the various women: Angel, Chaney, Ruth. A lot of women in your life, and a lot of lovely women, a lot of difficult women. Overall – and of course I want to hear the Jeannie story for the tape – but overall, how would you characterize your relationship with women?
With who?
Women, in general.
It was . . .
Jimmy and women.
I’ll tell you. The women, they were hungry.
They were hungry, he says.

Yeah, and all they wanted was, “You’re an entertainer, you’re making money, and give it to me.” Naturally most of them felt – the ones that I went out with, that’s the way most of them felt. I didn’t feel that that was what I wanted for life, so we didn’t get along. I just went ahead and lived my life. But the only women I’ve ever had that has shown me what a wife is is this young lady right here.
Jeannie.
Jeannie.
How did you meet Jeannie?

I was at – was it? – the Birdland on 52nd, when they moved from the other place. I was there. Jeannie and a friend of hers and mine came into Birdland at night, that I was there. I was introduced to Jeannie. What’s Steve’s last name?
Steve Nicholas.
Nichols?

However. He introduced me to Jeannie. That was it. It was over, because I dug her attitude first and how she was such a lady about – she’s out there in the streets with us, but she was a lady and acted that way. That’s what I respected about her.
You – in your mind, you had never had another woman who cared about helping you with your career.
No.
Not one of them.
No. Not any at all.
Not Catherine or Francis or Chaney or Eve or . . .

First – this is the first woman that ever took it upon herself to find out information, bring it to me. We’d discuss it. If it was good, she’d work on it for me. We’ve been successful in our relationship because of that, I feel. Right, Jeannie?
Let me ask you some general questions about the jazz life, that you’ve lived the jazz life your whole life.
Who?
The jazz life, by which I mean, you’re making it up as you go along. The jazz life is not – you’ve never lived a conventional life.
No.
You’ve always lived an unconventional life. Do you feel that you’ve been true to your art?
I’ve been what?
True to your art form.

Yes, I do. I’ve given it all that I have and will continue to give it all that I have. That’s my sincere determination, is to give it all that I have, because it hasn’t done me bad. Others outside of the business, they did me bad, but the business itself hasn’t done me bad, I don’t think. It’s just that persons who didn’t mean right, they caused problems that weren’t necessary. That’s where my problems began. It was other people. My family was a big innovator of that, the problems I had in the business. So that’s why I say, the business didn’t treat me bad. It would have been much better if I had had the sincerity from the folks I was dealing with, sincerity in the sense of nobody wanted to learn how they could help me or what could they do that would help me. That wasn’t – but their biggest reasons were, “Man, you got the money?” I said, “No, I don’t have no money.” “You got paid last night, didn’t you?” That was family as well as so-called friends in the street. That was the attitude, which interfered in a lot of ways with my thinking. That was a part of life I had to deal with. When I decided to drop that part, okay, things changed. But the force that helped them change was this little girl right here, Jeannie.
When you look, do you think you’ve been an unfor – do you think you’ve been a man who’s encountered a great deal of misfortune? Or a man who’s really been blessed?

A great deal of misfortune, you can say. It has been a great deal of misfortune. But if I’d had someone in the business who was serious about being in the business and doing the right thing, I know there would have been success out of it.

I know you’ve read deeply into Christian theology and also Eastern religion. So I know you’ve given a lot of thought to the meaning of God in our lives. Why do you think a guy like you – was a sweetheart and a loving disposition – has had this much misfortune imposed on you?
People prey on that. There’s people out there that prey on that.
That’s exactly what I’m talking about.

I didn’t – I ignored that. Out of ignoring that, I fell into the hands of many people who didn’t care about my career. What the hell? That wasn’t their business, and it wasn’t important to them. It was only important to me. But like I say, I ignored a lot of it. Out of ignoring a lot of it, it became a damage to me.
And also, do you feel as though you took care of your own business?
The best I could, yes. I also feel that I trusted too many people.
Ah, too trusting a heart.

I trusted too many people. It didn’t do me any good. It didn’t create success for me at all. But like I say, you give out, but you don’t give up. That was my attitude about the whole thing, and still is.

Because the truth is, you began to sing as a teenage, and at 82, you’re still singing, and there was no time when you didn’t sing. You had other jobs, but you always went back to the little club. So you have this tenacity, where you keep on coming back, keep on coming back, keep on coming back, keep on coming back. But when you look at the great stylists whose eras that you lived in – Lionel Hampton, Nat King Cole, Billy Eckstine, Ella, Dinah, Nancy Wilson, people whose styles have been so influenced by you, do you feel like you’ve been left out?

In a way, yes, but they had reason for leaving me out. I wasn’t important to them. So there. I had to understand that. Because I looked around. People like James Brown, they were friends. All those kids. They were popular, but they were friends where I was concerned, and they treated me as a friend. So the artists in the business treated me with respect.
As an equal.
[recording interrupted]

I was there that night that you were awarded the NEH Jazz Master award. Remember, in the hotel in New York, with – Nancy Wilson gave you the award. What did that mean to you? What was that evening like?
It meant a lot. It was like graduating at school or something. It’s like a graduation for me, to a better side of life.
Of course it must have been nice, the award was given by Nancy.

Yes, but I wondered why sometime. Why did they pick her to do that? Because it wasn’t necessary, and there was never any apologies for things that she did. So I just took it with a smile, kept on going.

When you think back to the years in Cleveland or L.A. or in Newark or in New York, and you want to warm your heart when you might feel bad from a physical point of view or a little sad, what memories do you conjure forth, do you bring up, that warm your heart and make you happy?
I think of my mother.
Yeah, I knew you were going to say that. That’s so sweet.

She would play the piano, and I’d hear this. Even since she’s been dead, I’ve heard the music. It’s always gospel. It’s always gospel, and it was a thrill listening to it and hearing it and singing it inside of myself.
What other warm memories do you bring up to comfort your heart when you feel bad, when you hurt?
Now I have something to feel good about, seriously. I feel that I have something to feel good about. We’re going to make it, huh?
When people – when you think of your concept of God, do you feel like – tell me just how you react to this phrase – do you feel like God has been good to you?
Oh my goodness, yes.
Good.
Yes sir. All the good that’s ever happened to me . . .
Comes from God.
I figure some people don’t stop and realize what it’s all about. They deny themselves of that trust and care that God gives.
So you’re grateful to God. You’ve . . .
Oh my Lord, yes.
I like to hear that. And you feel blessed.
Listen. How many times have I fell, and he picked me up. I look at it just like that. My trust [?] than it’s ever been before.

That’s a beautiful thing. When you think back over the large extent of your life, who are the great characters who stand out the most, the really most brilliant, the most charismatic, most colorful, most unforgettable characters? Were I to just ask you to name them, without giving it too much thought.
Bird.
Bird.
One of them. Dinah is another, because before Dinah passed, every time she had to do an important gig, the gig she was on she had to leave, she would call me to take her place.
That’s quite a compliment.
Oh yes. Listen. This goes back to the Flame . . .
In Detroit.
. . . in Detroit, and places like that. She’d always have a spot for me.
Had a spot for Jimmy.
I love her for it . . .
So we love Dinah.
. . . because it kept me alive. Now there’s another point where you can’t help but thank God, because with friends like that . . .

Let me ask you something else, before we run out of tape here, which is a big concept in your life. You’ll always be remembered in a lot of ways, but one of the ways you’ll be most remembered is in your notion of time and rhythm and how you have your sense of it. Throughout your career, you’ve been criticized and also applauded. On one hand, people love you for having such an individualistic sense of time. On the other hand, you’ve had people criticize you and in certain instances, like Charlie Mingus, get up and leave when they’re recording and saying . . .
Yeah, we were recording . . .
You go ahead and tell that story.
. . . and he threw the bass. He said, oh man, this cat he ain’t doing – can’t sing.
This is the ’50s.
The other cats had to go get him. They told him – they said, they can’t be there when you get there. That was the way they expressed it to him about me.
To Mingus.
Yeah. I’m saying, here is a cat who – time was no problem for him. No. So why did he pick me to say the things he said at the session.

But were you ever challenged to the point where you went, maybe they’re right? Maybe my timing’s off? Maybe I have to pay more attention to the meter and be – keep a stricter sense of time? Did you ever have those doubts? Did you ever think . . .? You always knew that you were going to take your time.
Yeah, I knew that worked out well. I was going to sing the song that way.
No matter what.
And it seemed to work. It works.
So you had enough people who appreciated . . .
Yeah.
. . . your individualism.
Yeah, my audiences. It started out like that for me. They appreciate what I was doing . . .
So in other words . . .
. . . and I worked hard at it.
So in other words, part of the reason you were able to stick to your individualism is because your early responses had been very positive.
Yes.
When you did Everybody’s Somebody’s Fool with the Hampton band, the audiences loved it and went crazy, and they didn’t care if you were behind the beat. They didn’t – they just . . .
They didn’t know about that.
They didn’t know about that. What they heard was your heart, and their hearts connected to your heart, so they went crazy.
And I figure, if people listen to the lyrics . . .
They’d really get it.
. . . they’d understand that the singer’s telling them a story.
In his own way.
Yes.

I guess what I was thinking was, in the case of Lester Young and Mingus, two of the most highly individual people in the history of jazz, getting kicked in the ass by them early on and still maintaining your integrity, I think is impressive, to me. The other thing I wanted to ask you was, the other challenges of your life – we’ve touched on the women. We’ve touched on the career – but the other challenges – I remember the story that went around about you, when Everybody’s Somebody’s Fool came out, and people were saying, “That’s not a man. That’s a lesbian in drag.” Jimmy, you must have heard those stories. Did you hear those stories? Or not?
Yeah but, again, like I say, you ignore it . . .
So that didn’t hurt you.

. . . and move on. You have to move on. You can’t let those things stop you. You hear them, and you are disappointed that it’s being said, but that’s just a disappointment, and you ignore it. You learn to ignore it. The main thing is, you don’t want it a part of your life. You don’t want it a part of your life. So you learn how to ignore those things when they come about.
So you don’t feel as though you had been taunted more than you could take. You felt as though you were equipped to handle the taunts and handle the teasing.
Yes. Exactly. I never had a confusion with a person about things like that.
I see. So sexually, you always knew who you were . . .
Right.
. . . and were confident about it.

My mother was very strict with my brother and I about, “Get up boy. Stand up there.” You don’t drop down to other people’s things. No. You don’t do that. She was very strict about that. Yeah. And if I see her, she’s saying, “If I catch you ever, I’d tear your butt up.” And she would have.
Do you mean by that, catch you with a man? Or just catch you . . .?
Oh, anything derogative in life. “If I catch it, you going to get it.” That’s what that – that was her slogan. That’s her way. I didn’t want to get it, so I didn’t drop down to it.
That should be the name of this interview. You look like you’re getting a little tired?
A little bit.
All right. I think we should dedicate this interview to your mother . . .
Thank you.
. . . and to Jeannie . . .
And to Jeannie.
. . . the two women, one of whom gave you life, and the other of whom continues to give you life.
Yes, yes. You got it just right.
All right. On that happy note . . .
(transcribed and edited by Barry Kernfeld)

segments.title: Opening and birth date
segments.summary: Ritz opens the session in Las Vegas on September 23, 2008; Scott gives his birth date, July 17, 1925.

segments.title: First music: radio, magazines and the Hampton band
segments.summary: Scott remembers hearing music at about 10 on radio, mentions Hampton, Dinah Washington and lyric magazines, and says the business taught him it was serious.

segments.title: Radio bands as champions of the music
segments.summary: Without record players at home, the family gathered around the radio for Dorsey, Goodman and others.

segments.title: Mother's piano and gospel singing at home
segments.summary: His mother played stride piano, the children sang gospel through the vents, and she corrected him as a teacher.

segments.title: The family quartet
segments.summary: Scott, Kenneth, Nadine and Adore sing as the family quartet.

segments.title: Cleveland and his mother the seamstress
segments.summary: He grew up in cold Cleveland; his mother was a seamstress who loved her Singer machine.

segments.title: His father the asphalt worker
segments.summary: His father laid and graded asphalt but was negligent, angry and brutal toward his family.

segments.title: Kallmann Syndrome and the clinic at Western Reserve
segments.summary: He and his brother were born with Kallmann Syndrome; his mother took them to the clinic and refused experimental drugs.

segments.title: Living with the syndrome in silence
segments.summary: He never discussed it with other kids or his brother; his mother told him to live with it, and he criticizes how little boys are taught.

segments.chapter: Mother's death and breakup of the family
segments.title: How his mother was killed
segments.summary: At 13 he learned his mother was struck by a car while saving his sister; he recalls skipping school that day.

segments.chapter: Mother's death and breakup of the family
segments.title: Detention home and the father's absence
segments.summary: After her death the grandmother sent the children to a detention home; the siblings scheme and the father does not step up.

segments.chapter: Mother's death and breakup of the family
segments.title: Foster care and music as salvation
segments.summary: A social worker places the brothers in foster homes; he says his interest in music kept him from falling apart.

segments.chapter: Mother's death and breakup of the family
segments.title: Family drifts apart and why he left for Las Vegas
segments.summary: His mother's words held him together while his siblings drifted; foster homes in Cleveland and Youngstown, then return at 16 and later move away.

segments.title: Gospel radio and Paul Robeson as a storyteller
segments.summary: Sunday gospel radio comforted him, and Robeson taught him to make a song mean something; Dinah as champion.

segments.title: His father's drinking clubs
segments.summary: He did not go to his father's clubs, which were just drinking and menacing talk.

segments.title: First live bands in Cleveland theaters
segments.summary: Theaters brought Dinah, Lunceford, Hines and Calloway, his first live music; he took busboy and hotel jobs.

segments.title: First time singing: valet for tap dancers, and Lester Young
segments.summary: Valeting for Lem Neal and Dickie Sims, he sang Talk of the Town on a gig and was told by Lester Young to go back to the dressing room.

segments.title: Why Lester said it, and later friendship
segments.summary: Scott decides Lester meant not to get a big head, and says they later became great friends.

segments.title: Hampton discovers him in Milwaukee
segments.summary: Hampton and members come to hear him in Milwaukee and Gladys Hampton arranges to hire him.

segments.title: Songs with Hampton and touring to Hawaii
segments.summary: He sang Why Was I Born and Everybody's Somebody's Fool, and traveled widely including to Hawaii.

segments.title: Hampton's music and band repertoire
segments.summary: Hampton's vibes behind his singing, the hard-swinging hits, and Winnie Brown as guest.

segments.title: Betty Carter and the roots of his stage presence
segments.summary: Betty was a good showman; his gestures came from his school coach Mr. Todd and Miss McGrath, plus Judy Garland.

segments.title: The story of Everybody's Somebody's Fool
segments.summary: Regina Adams gave him the song at the Apollo, Hampton had it arranged, and the record came out without his name.

segments.title: Leaving Hampton over pay and the Decca record
segments.summary: He left after a dispute; he got nothing from the record because Hampton held the Decca contract.

segments.title: Back in Cleveland: drugstore and first club production
segments.summary: He worked at Curlander's drug store, sang some local gigs and produced a show at Cedar Gardens.

segments.title: Tadd Dameron and the Cleveland scene
segments.summary: Tadd Dameron played piano for him and taught him keys; his brother Caesar played tenor.

segments.title: Cafe Tia Juana and hearing Ella, Billie, Sarah and Dinah
segments.summary: The jazz-only Tia Juana hosted the great singers; Scott came prepared and never compared himself.

segments.title: Teddy Reig and the Roost label
segments.summary: Teddy Reig, around Basie and the bands, got him recorded for Roost with his own name on the label.

segments.title: No say over material at Roost; Johnnie Ray
segments.summary: Roost brought songs they wanted for hits; he also recalls Johnnie Ray sitting in at the Apollo.

segments.title: Herman Lubinsky and Savoy in Newark
segments.summary: Lubinsky invited him in Newark, Freddie Mendelsohn arranged the studio, and again he did not pick material.

segments.title: Contracts, no lawyers and Savoy's reputation
segments.summary: He had no lawyer or manager and learned the contract too late; lawyers avoided Lubinsky.

segments.title: Big Maybelle
segments.summary: He and Maybelle both came from Cleveland; she was like a little sister, harmed by her boyfriend and drugs.

segments.title: Little Willie John
segments.summary: Willie John wanted to learn his ballads, and Scott describes his gangster-style short-man pose.

segments.title: No royalties and Lubinsky's treatment of artists
segments.summary: He earned no royalties and session costs went unpaid; Lubinsky mistreated everybody.

segments.chapter: Ray Charles and the shelved album
segments.title: Ray Charles invites him to California
segments.summary: Via Joe Adams, Ray wants to record him; for the first time he is allowed to pick tunes.

segments.chapter: Ray Charles and the shelved album
segments.title: Making the Ray Charles album
segments.summary: Arrangers Gerald Wilson and Marty Paich, Ray at the piano on every track, and freedom to sing.

segments.chapter: Ray Charles and the shelved album
segments.title: Aside about Tony Gumina and the album cover
segments.summary: A brief aside on Tony Gumina, then the cover with a male model that did not bother him.

segments.chapter: Ray Charles and the shelved album
segments.title: Lubinsky blocks the album
segments.summary: Lubinsky threatened Ray, who shelved the record to protect himself.

segments.chapter: Ray Charles and the shelved album
segments.title: Taking his father home and losing Mary Ann
segments.summary: He drove his father back to Cleveland; Mary Ann left with their adopted son and he returned to Cleveland.

segments.chapter: Ray Charles and the shelved album
segments.title: Singing Embraceable You with Charlie Parker
segments.summary: Bird invited him up at Birdland; Columbia recorded it and he was not paid.

segments.chapter: Cleveland lean years and The Source
segments.title: Busboy jobs, agent Jimmy Evans and his brother
segments.summary: Back in Cleveland he busboyed, resented an agent who took money, and his brother Kenneth lived with him.

segments.chapter: Cleveland lean years and The Source
segments.title: Joel Dorn and The Source
segments.summary: Atlantic's Joel Dorn let him pick songs, but the album was unpromoted and bore a woman on the cover.

segments.chapter: Cleveland lean years and The Source
segments.title: The hotel accident
segments.summary: In 1971 as shipping clerk he fell backwards on the thirteenth floor, starting his injuries and a jobless period.

segments.title: Freddy Mendelsohn calls for Can't We Begin Again
segments.summary: Mendelsohn offered a Savoy album and paid about $10,000, more than Lubinsky would have.

segments.title: Declared dead on Newark radio
segments.summary: Bill Cook's show, Newark as his town, Joe Pesci, and the calls after he went on air to say he was alive.

segments.title: Baby Grand and no steady income
segments.summary: He worked Newark, Long Island and the Baby Grands but earned no steady living, and family never came.

segments.title: Meeting Doc Pomus
segments.summary: He met Doc Pomus at the Baby Grand, visited his home, and Doc's Billboard letter went unknown to him.

segments.title: Doc's last calls and singing at his funeral
segments.summary: Doc kept in touch until the end; Scott sang Someone to Watch Over Me at the funeral.

segments.title: From the funeral to a Warner Bros. contract
segments.summary: Attention from the funeral led to a Warner contract and producer Tommy LiPuma.

segments.title: Keeping expectations down
segments.summary: He says he fights getting excited after many broken hopes.

segments.title: Choosing songs with LiPuma
segments.summary: He and Tommy created the songs together with no material imposed.

segments.title: Touring with Lou Reed
segments.summary: He met Lou through Doc, toured England and Europe, and rejected his advances amid his jealousy.

segments.title: Twin Peaks appearance
segments.summary: Ritz confuses Byrne and Lynch; Scott describes appearing on Twin Peaks with strings recorded but unreleased.

segments.title: Fantasy albums and Todd Barkin
segments.summary: He says Barkin and Fantasy did not respect his ability.

segments.title: Women in his life and meeting Jeannie
segments.summary: Earlier women wanted his money; Jeannie, introduced at Birdland, was the first to help his career.

segments.title: True to his art, misfortune and trusting too many
segments.summary: He says the business did not treat him badly; people and family did, and he trusted too many.

segments.title: Being left out and the NEA Jazz Master award
segments.summary: He feels left out but treated as a friend by peers; the award evening felt like a graduation.

segments.title: Mother's memory and gratitude to God
segments.summary: He recalls his mother's piano and says God has been good to him.

segments.title: Unforgettable characters: Bird and Dinah
segments.summary: He names Bird and Dinah, who had him fill in for her on gigs, as most unforgettable.

segments.title: Time and phrasing, and Mingus walking out
segments.summary: Mingus threw his bass at a session over his sense of time, but audiences understood the story in the lyrics.

segments.title: Taunts, sexuality and his mother's strictness
segments.summary: He ignored rumors about Everybody's Somebody's Fool and says his mother's strictness shaped him.

segments.title: Closing dedication
segments.summary: Ritz dedicates the interview to Scott's mother and Jeannie.
